name: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
title: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
answer: Threat modelling for legal AI is the structured practice of identifying what can go wrong when AI systems are used in legal work, from client intake and legal research to contract review, e-discovery, and drafting. It covers threats to confidentiality, attorney-client privilege, work product, data integrity, and the reliability of legal outputs, not just classic software vulnerabilities. The scope includes the AI model, the prompts and retrieval data, the surrounding application, the people who use it, and the legal workflows it touches. Because legal AI often handles sensitive matter data, threat modelling must consider both deliberate attacks and accidental failures such as hallucinated citations or overbroad data exposure.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Legal AI systems typically run on a stack of foundation models, sometimes hosted by an external provider and sometimes deployed in a private cloud or on premises. Around the model sit retrieval stores, vector databases, document management systems, matter management platforms, and identity and access controls. Threat modelling must map data flows across these components, including API calls, prompt logs, embeddings, fine tuning data, and any human review queues. The infrastructure may also include third party tools for OCR, translation, or e-discovery, each of which adds its own supply chain and access path.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Teams usually start with a data flow diagram and a set of trust boundaries, then apply a framework such as STRIDE or MITRE ATLAS to enumerate threats. For legal AI, that means asking how an attacker could manipulate a prompt, poison a retrieval corpus, extract confidential text through model outputs, or cause a model to cite a non-existent case. The method also includes abuse cases, such as a user trying to bypass privilege filters or a vendor using client data for training without permission. Findings are ranked by likelihood and impact, then tied to controls like input validation, output filtering, access logging, and human review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Threat modelling for legal AI must account for professional responsibility rules, data protection law, and contractual duties of confidentiality. Provenance matters because legal teams need to know which model version, training data, and retrieval sources produced an output, and whether the output can be audited later. The site tracks 215 compliance and regulation pages and 6,946 state AI bills, which reflect the fast moving patchwork of rules that can affect how legal AI is deployed. Risk registers typically record who owns each threat, what evidence shows a control works, and how incidents are reported to clients or regulators.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Threat modelling for legal AI is moving from one-off reviews toward continuous monitoring, because models, prompts, and retrieval sources change frequently. Expect more attention to agentic systems that can browse, draft, and file documents, which expands the attack surface beyond a single chat interface. Regulatory and case law developments, including the 147 active AI lawsuits and 92 intellectual property matters tracked by this site, will keep pressure on provenance and disclosure practices. The field is also likely to see more shared threat libraries and standardised control mappings so that legal teams can compare notes without starting from scratch.
